# Phase 0: harnesses and prerequisites

Part of the [`ci-doctor`](../../SKILL.md) hub. What [Phase 0](../phases/phase-0-know-your-harness-and-your-helpers.md) needs from the guide and the reference READMEs, copied from them so the phase runs where only the skills are installed. Each part links its source.

## Harnesses: parallel agents and recurring work

From [docs/harnesses.md](../../../../docs/harnesses.md). Which harness you are, and what it can run: subagents, worktrees and schedules.

This page covers how to run several agents at once—each in its own checkout—and how to schedule the standing work in [guide section 16](../../../../docs/pages/16-standing-automations.md) across the harnesses we know. [Phase 0](../phases/phase-0-know-your-harness-and-your-helpers.md) asks you to check which capabilities your harness provides; prefer whatever the user already uses. Working with a single agent and no schedule is completely valid: every schedule is opt-in, and the default follow-up is a manual, read-only check.

Harnesses evolve quickly. Every entry below was verified against its documentation in November 2026. Check the linked docs before relying on a feature, and if you can't confirm it exists, say so and fall back to a more portable option.

### What you need from a harness

- **Parallel work:** The ability to start child agents in isolated git worktrees and branches so their edits and test runs don't collide, ideally with a second model available for reading. Always start each worktree from an explicit ref—the default branch for independent work.
- **A schedule,** choosing from four options, each with its own identity and cost profile:

  | Kind | Runs where | Signed in as | Costs |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | Interactive session loop | Inside an open session | The session's account | Model usage; stops when the session ends |
  | Cloud agent job | A fresh clone on the harness's servers | Its own identity, with credentials scoped to the job | Model usage, plus the provider's job pricing |
  | Script-only GitHub Actions cron | A fresh runner | The workflow's `GITHUB_TOKEN` and the permissions you grant | Runner minutes; no model usage |
  | Host timer (systemd, cron) | Your machine, with its local files | The intended user, with their config home and `PATH` | The machine; model usage if it invokes an agent |

  Prefer a plain script for any deterministic task. Use a model only when the job requires judgement.
- **Limits that hold:** The agreed cap on concurrent agents, the machine's test-slot cap ([guide section 14](../../../../docs/pages/14-local-speed-and-many-agents-on-one-machine.md)), and scheduled-run permissions scoped no wider than the job needs.
- **A plan for the first run:** Name who inspects the first eligible result, and define what happens if no run starts.

### Skills folder and instruction file

Each harness looks for skills in its own folder and loads its own startup instruction file. Skills copied by hand go into `<skills-dir>` (see [`skills/README.md`](../../../README.md#install)). A plugin install keeps its own copy; put the [agent-knowledge snippet](../agent-knowledge/README.md) in the instruction file below.

| Harness | Repo skills folder (`<skills-dir>`) | User skills folder | Instruction file |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `.claude/skills/<skill>/SKILL.md` | `~/.claude/skills/` | `CLAUDE.md` or `.claude/CLAUDE.md`; reads `AGENTS.md` when no `CLAUDE.md` exists, or via a `@AGENTS.md` import |
| Codex CLI | `.agents/skills/`, in any folder from the working directory up to the repo root | `~/.agents/skills/` | `AGENTS.md` (`AGENTS.override.md` in the same folder wins), one per folder from the root down, plus `~/.codex/AGENTS.md` |
| T3 Code | The folders of the provider each thread runs | The same | The same |

Docs: [Claude Code skills](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills), [Claude Code's instruction files](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory), [Codex skills](https://developers.openai.com/codex/skills), and [Codex's AGENTS.md](https://developers.openai.com/codex/guides/agents-md). A single `AGENTS.md`, imported from `CLAUDE.md`, serves both.

### Claude Code

- **Subagents** run in their own context and return a summary; several can run in parallel, in the background or foreground. Define reusable subagents as Markdown files in `.claude/agents/` (project) or `~/.claude/agents/` (user). Docs: [subagents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents).
- **Worktrees:** Setting `isolation: worktree` in a subagent's frontmatter runs it in a temporary git worktree, which is removed if nothing changes. It branches from the repo's default branch unless `worktree.baseRef` points to your current work. Docs: [choose the base branch](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/worktrees#choose-the-base-branch).
- **`/loop`** reruns a prompt on an interval (or at a cadence Claude chooses) inside an open session. Tasks are session-scoped, stop when the session exits, and expire after seven days if recurring. Well suited for watching a run or PR, not for standing jobs. Docs: [run prompts on a schedule](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/scheduled-tasks).
- **`/schedule` (cloud scheduled tasks, formerly routines)** runs a saved prompt against a fresh clone of the repo—on a schedule, via API call, or on a GitHub event—even with your machine off. Because it doesn't share your local files or config home, configure its identity and credentials specifically for the job. Good for the slow-tests campaign or a docs drift sweep, not for local machine timers. Docs: [scheduled tasks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/routines).
- **Desktop scheduled tasks** run on your machine with its files and tools while the desktop app is open.
- **Headless:** Use `claude -p "<prompt>"` for scripts, CI workflows, and timers. Docs: [headless mode](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless).

### Codex CLI

- **`codex exec "<task>"`** runs non-interactively without the TUI, writing progress to stderr and the final message to stdout. It is read-only by default; pass `--sandbox workspace-write` to allow edits. Use `--json` to stream events, `-o <file>` to save the final message, and `codex exec resume --last` to continue a session. Docs: [non-interactive mode](https://developers.openai.com/codex/non-interactive-mode).
- **Parallel work:** Launch one `codex exec` per git worktree, each from its own directory, and wait for all of them to finish. Always name the starting ref—otherwise `git worktree add` branches from your current `HEAD`: `git fetch origin && git worktree add ../<repo>-<task> -b <branch> origin/<default-branch>`.
- **In CI:** Use [`openai/codex-action`](https://github.com/openai/codex-action). Pass the provider key only as the action's input, never as a job-level environment variable in a workflow that executes repository code. The action protects the key only when configured with its documented privilege safeguard (`safety-strategy: drop-sudo` or a configured unprivileged user) on a compatible runner—read [its credential safeguards](https://github.com/openai/codex-action/blob/main/docs/security.md#protecting-your-openai_api_key) before enabling it. Let a separate job, with its own scoped credentials and no model key, apply any resulting changes.

### T3 Code

[T3 Code](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code) runs Claude, Codex, and other providers' agents in threads, each of which can have its own git worktree. That much is covered in its public documentation.

Some builds also expose orchestration tools to agents: starting a child agent on a named provider and model (optionally in its own worktree) and scheduling a prompt on a cadence. Tool names and options vary by build and aren't in the public user docs. Check your build's tool list before relying on them, stay within the agreed agent cap, and note which build you checked. Without them, fall back to the plain recipes above and below: one worktree per task via `git worktree add`, plus each harness's headless command.

### GitHub Actions cron

A scheduled workflow (`on: schedule:` plus `workflow_dispatch:`) runs in a fresh checkout and is the most portable option.

- **Script-only first.** The sweep in [`templates/github/`](../../../../templates/github/README.md) is a script-only cron: it dispatches ordinary CI without running an agent. Use that pattern for anything a script can decide.
- **Headless agent when needed.** When a job genuinely requires judgement, run the harness's headless command and pass the provider key only to the step or action that needs it.
- **Don't trust cron timing.** GitHub starts scheduled runs late or skips them under load. Have a merge or a dispatch trigger missed runs, as our sweep does ([guide section 5](../../../../docs/pages/05-tiers-what-runs-where.md#cron-is-not-a-scheduler-you-can-trust)).
- **Least privilege.** Grant only the permissions the job requires, and let a separate job without the model key apply changes, as in Codex's auto-fix pattern. Both [Claude Code's GitHub Actions](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/github-actions) and [`openai/codex-action`](https://github.com/openai/codex-action) document their setups.
- **Count both costs.** You pay runner minutes at your CI provider's rate, plus model usage if the job runs an agent. Include both in the budget.

### A machine of your own: systemd timers or cron

For jobs that need access to local machine files—such as the CI-records collector or the temp and Rust sweeps—use a systemd user timer or a crontab entry running a plain script (or the agent's headless command if the job needs judgement).

- **Set the user and environment explicitly.** Timers run with a minimal environment. Run them as the user who owns the job and set `HOME`, `PATH`, and the model CLI's config directory to match that user's interactive sessions; otherwise the CLI will run signed out.
- **Survive logout.** Enable `loginctl enable-linger` for systemd user timers, and set `Persistent=true` so missed timers catch up when the machine comes back online.
- **Examples:** [`scripts/records/`](../../../../scripts/records/README.md) and [`scripts/local/`](../../../../scripts/local/README.md) ship `.service` and `.timer` unit files, and [`scripts/local/README.md`](../../../../scripts/local/README.md#what-the-machine-needs) lists the host prerequisites. Install them only after the plan approves them.

### Which to use

| Job | Best fit |
| --- | --- |
| Engineers working briefs in parallel | Subagents or child tasks in worktrees; `codex exec` per worktree |
| Watching one run or PR for an hour | `/loop` or your harness's PR watcher |
| The slow-tests campaign, the docs drift sweep | A cloud agent job with its own scoped identity, or GitHub Actions cron running the agent headless |
| The CI-records collector, temp and Rust sweeps, the spend watcher | A script on a systemd timer or service on the machine |
| A follow-up check at a main-only job's first run | A manual, read-only check by a named person or agent at a set time; a one-off scheduled task if the user approves one |

## Local: fast feedback, and many agents on one machine

From [scripts/local/README.md](../../../../scripts/local/README.md). The conditional prerequisites, for a plan that uses the local scripts.

### What the machine needs

Each piece is optional. Check the ones you use:

| For | Install and check |
| --- | --- |
| Test slots | Perl with `Fcntl` (for `flock`). Without Perl, `test-slots.ts` warns and runs the file with no slot, so the bound is silently gone. Check, with no other test runs on the machine: in **both** shells set the same temporary cap and pool (`export TEST_SLOTS=1`, the same `PROJECT`), hold a slot in one with a slow test file, start a second run in the other, and see it wait. Then go back to the common launch setting. |
| The housekeeping timers and the spend watcher | Linux with `/proc`, Bash 4+, GNU coreutils and findutils, Node 24 or later, and a working systemd user manager (`systemctl --user status`). Run `loginctl enable-linger` if they must run while you're logged out. Give each unit a `PATH` holding the CLIs it calls (`git`, `gh`, `blacksmith`). |
| The Rust sweep | Node 24 or later, `git`, and `gh` logged in with read access to the repo's pull requests |
| Anything else | On macOS or another OS, adapt the scripts and use its scheduler (launchd, cron), or mark them as not applying. |

Make the folders the install steps below write to: `mkdir -p ~/.local/bin ~/.config/systemd/user`.
